title: Strong
description: The strong element for genuinely important text, with a full strong vs b comparison.
subject: html
html:
The <strong> tag marks text of genuine strong importance, seriousness, or urgency — not just text you want to look bold.

Syntax

<strong>important text</strong>

Basic Example

<p><strong>Warning:</strong> deleting your account cannot be undone.</p>

Browser output: "Warning:" renders in bold — visually the same as <b>, but this time the boldness reflects real importance a reader shouldn't skip.

How It Works

The browser applies font-weight: bold by default, exactly like <b>. The difference is entirely semantic — assistive technology and other machines can use <strong> to identify content that genuinely matters, in a way they can't with purely presentational bold.

Important Attributes

AttributePurpose
— none —Only universal global attributes apply

Real-World Example

<form>
    <label for="email">Email <strong>(required)</strong></label>
    <input type="email" id="email" name="email" required>
</form>

Flagging a required field, a security warning, or a critical instruction — content a user genuinely should not miss.

Comparison: b vs strong (quick recap)

<b> is stylistic bold with no meaning attached; <strong> is a semantic signal of real importance. They render identically by default but mean different things to machines. Full comparison table: Bold Text.

Common Mistakes

  • Using <strong> and <b> interchangeably just because they look the same — the meaning is the entire point
  • Nesting <strong><strong>text</strong></strong> expecting "extra bold" — nesting doesn't stack visual weight, it just adds redundant importance markers
  • Overusing <strong> across most of a page's text, which dilutes its meaning until nothing feels important anymore

Best Practices

  • Reserve <strong> for content that would genuinely be a problem to miss — warnings, required fields, critical instructions
  • Keep it rare enough that it still stands out both visually and semantically

Accessibility Considerations

Screen readers may change vocal emphasis or pitch when reading <strong> content, depending on the reader/voice — a real functional benefit that purely visual bold (<b>) does not reliably provide.

SEO Considerations

There's a long-running, largely unconfirmed belief that <strong> content gets extra search-ranking weight. Treat it as, at most, a very minor signal — never a substitute for genuinely good, well-structured content.

Browser & Modern HTML Notes

HTML5 redefined <strong> from "extra-strong bold styling" (where nesting used to visually stack) into a pure importance/urgency signal, matching how it's used in practice today.

Mini Practice

  1. Add a <strong> warning to a form about an irreversible action.
  2. Rewrite a paragraph that overuses <strong> on nearly every sentence, keeping it only on the one genuinely important point.
